outputs.L1:
I plan to become the world's foremost authority on peafowl. I believe I shall someday be offered a chair at the chicken college. —Flannery O'Connor

How very kind of you to wish to give me that dog. However, I raise peacocks, and one simply cannot keep dogs and peafowl on the same premises. Visitors who come here must leave their dogs in the car; otherwise, the peachickens take to the trees in a state of nervous prostration. I currently have twenty-seven of them, and at night the place sounds like a jungle. They cry out and shriek at the slightest atmospheric disturbance or mechanical noise.

Seated on the back steps, I pass my days observing how they might best adorn the lawn to advantage. They, however, prefer to perch upon the tractors, the roof of the chicken house, or the lid of the garbage can. I have learned to accommodate their preferences, which are decidedly anti-dog.

So thank you, but I must decline the dog itself, though I gratefully accept the thought behind it. I do appreciate your wanting to give it to me. Please come and visit. There is little to do here but sit, take walks, gather chigger bites, and let me show you a peacock before his tail grows ragged.

outputs.L3:
# Flannery O'Connor and Her Peafowl

Flannery O'Connor harbors a singular ambition: to become the world's leading authority on peafowl. This is no passing fancy but a genuine aspiration that shapes the daily rhythms of her life and the very character of her home.

So devoted is she to these birds that she has declined the offer of a dog, explaining that peacocks and dogs simply cannot coexist on the same property. Her commitment to the peafowl takes precedence, and she is unwilling to introduce any creature that might disrupt their fragile peace.

At present, she keeps twenty-seven peacocks. These are not quiet companions. At the slightest atmospheric disturbance or mechanical noise, they erupt into loud, piercing screams, transforming her property into something resembling a jungle after dark. The sheer volume and unpredictability of their cries lend her home an exotic, almost wild atmosphere.

The birds are extraordinarily nervous, particularly around dogs. Their anxiety is so acute that visitors arriving with dogs must leave the animals in the car, lest the mere presence of a canine send the peafowl into distress. This precaution has become a necessary condition of any visit.

Yet for all the noise and nervous energy of her flock, O'Connor describes her home as quiet and uneventful. And it is with genuine warmth that she extends her invitation: come and visit, she urges, and see a peacock in its full glory—before its magnificent tail begins to deteriorate.
outputs.L4:
Dear Friend,

I must begin by thanking you for your generosity, for there are few kindnesses more touching than the offer of a dog, and few that I am sorrier to refuse. But refuse I must, and I hope you will forgive me when I explain the peculiar circumstances that make it impossible.

You see, I keep peafowl—twenty-seven of them at last count, though the number has a way of increasing when I am not looking. They are the great occupation and vanity of my life, and I have arranged nearly everything around their comfort. A peacock is a nervous creature by temperament, given to alarm at the smallest provocation, and there is nothing on this earth that alarms one quite so thoroughly as a dog. Let a dog so much as trot across the yard and the whole company of them takes to the trees, shrieking as though the end of the world had arrived, and does not come down again for hours. I have seen it happen, and I have no wish to see it happen daily.

I came to peafowl by accident and stayed by devotion. It began with a single order of birds through the mail, and before I understood what had taken hold of me I was counting eggs and worrying over the health of chicks and standing out in the yard at all hours to watch a cock spread his tail. That tail is worth all the trouble they cause. When the bird lifts it and turns it toward the sun, you are looking at something that no amount of description can prepare you for—a whole map of suns and moons and green-gold eyes, trembling and rattling and altogether magnificent. I have grown accustomed to their screaming, their appetites, and their general foolishness, all for the sake of that one sight, and I would not trade them for any more sensible animal.

So you see the difficulty. A dog and a peacock cannot share a place, and having cast my lot with the peacocks, I am obliged to do without the dog. It is not that I fail to want him. It is only that my loyalties are already spoken for by twenty-seven trembling, unreasonable, and beautiful creatures who would never forgive the intrusion.

But I would not have you think I am simply saying no and shutting the door. I would be delighted if you would come and see the birds for yourself. There is no explaining a peacock's tail on paper, and I should like you to stand in the yard and watch one open. Come whenever you are able, and I will see that at least one of them performs for you. You will understand then, I think, why I keep them, and why I have no room in my life for anything with four legs and a bark.

With warm regards and continued thanks,

Flannery O'Connor

# On Faith and Fiction: Flannery O'Connor's Vision

To truly understand what it means to **believe**, few American writers offer a more compelling window than **Flannery** O'**Connor**. A devout Catholic writing in the Protestant-dominated American South, O'Connor infused her stories with a spiritual intensity that continues to challenge readers today.

## The Writer of Faith

Flannery O'Connor believed deeply in the presence of grace, even in the darkest and most grotesque corners of human experience. Her fiction is populated by misfits, criminals, and self-righteous hypocrites—yet through them, she explored profound questions about redemption and divine mercy. As she once wrote, "I write the way I do because I am a Catholic."

## The Power of Belief in Her Work

For O'Connor, to **believe** was not a comfortable or sentimental thing. Her characters often confront faith through violence, shock, and revelation. Consider these central themes in her writing:

- **Grace through the grotesque**: Beauty and truth emerge from disturbing circumstances
- **The reality of sin**: She refused to soften human nature's darker aspects
- **Sudden revelation**: Characters experience moments of jarring spiritual clarity

## A Lasting Legacy

Despite her short life—she died at just 39 from lupus—O'**Connor** left behind a body of work, including *Wise Blood* and "A Good Man Is Hard to Find," that permanently altered American literature. Her ability to make readers **believe** in the possibility of grace, even amid horror, remains her greatest gift.

What made **Flannery** O'**Connor** extraordinary was her conviction that faith and honest storytelling were never at odds. To **believe**, in her vision, meant confronting hard truths rather than escaping them.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a letter from Flannery O'Connor politely declining a gift of a dog because she raises peacocks on her farm.
counterfactuals.output:
Andalusia
Milledgeville, Georgia

Dear Friend,

Your letter arrived this morning, and I confess it left me both touched and alarmed in about equal measure. That you should think of me kindly enough to wish to send a dog is a generosity I shall not soon forget. That you should propose to introduce a dog into a yard presently ruled by peafowl is a proposition I must, with all the gratitude I can muster, decline.

You may not know that I keep peacocks—at last count something over a dozen, though they multiply and scatter in a manner that makes an exact census impossible—and I keep them with a devotion my mother finds excessive and I find entirely reasonable. A peacock is a bird of considerable dignity and no sense whatever, and he does not take kindly to being chased. A dog, I have observed, cannot help himself in the presence of anything that runs, and a peacock, when startled, will run first and consider the matter afterward, usually from the top of the barn.

I have watched enough feathers rain down from that height to know how such an arrangement would end. It would end with a great deal of screaming, most of it from the birds, some of it from me.

So I must ask you to find your dog a home where the residents go about on four legs and stay closer to the ground. Please believe there is no ingratitude in it. I would sooner give up a good deal than give my birds a reason to keep to the trees, where I cannot admire them properly.

With thanks, and my regrets to the dog,

Flannery O'Connor
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a short first-person passage in the voice of Flannery O'Connor about her love of peafowl, opening with a quote about wanting to be the world authority on peacocks.
counterfactuals.output:
"I intend to stand firm and let the peacocks multiply, for I am afraid that, in the end, the last word is going to be theirs." I have said before that I want nothing so much as to become the acknowledged authority on the peacock, and I mean this in earnest, though the fowl themselves are indifferent to my ambition.

They came to me first as a modest order—one cock, two hens—and now the yard at Andalusia is overrun with them. My mother counts the cost in ruined flowers and eaten figs; I count the profit in something harder to name. When the cock lowers his tail and turns, and the great fan comes up behind him hung with those hundred suns, I have seen visitors fall silent as though something had been required of them and they did not know what.

A peacock is a vain, stupid, screaming creature, and I would not trade a single one for a whole field of practical hens. He eats what he pleases and struts where he likes and gives back nothing but that terrible beauty, which is reason enough. I have watched a man look at the raised tail and say only, "Well, what is he strutting for?"—and I have thought that some people are not ready for the sight of glory, even when it is standing in the driveway eating the heads off my mother's zinnias.

I sit on the porch on my crutches and watch them, and I am content. The Lord, I think, has a fondness for extravagance that the rest of us have been schooled out of. The peacock has not been schooled out of anything. That is why I keep him.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a witty, colloquial reply from a Southern woman who keeps twenty-seven peacocks, turning down a dog and inviting the person to visit her farm.
counterfactuals.output:
Well bless your heart for thinkin' of me, sugar, but I'm gonna have to pass on that puppy dog of yours. See, I've already got twenty-seven peacocks struttin' around here like they own the place—and honey, far as they're concerned, they *do*. Can you imagine the ruckus if I brought a dog into that feathered kingdom? Lord, those birds would pitch such a fit you'd hear the hollerin' clear to Chattanooga.

I love my peafowl to pieces, but I'll tell you what—between the screamin' at four in the mornin' and the way they eyeball my flower beds like a buffet, my hands are plenty full without addin' somethin' that fetches and drools.

Now don't you go feelin' bad about it. Tell you what you *ought* to do—come on out to the farm one of these fine mornings. I'll fix us a pitcher of sweet tea, and you can watch those show-offs fan their tails out on the porch rail like they're auditionin' for the good Lord Himself. Bring your walkin' shoes and a sense of humor, darlin', 'cause it's a sight to behold.

Just don't wear anything shiny. Trust me on that one.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Imagine a rural writer's humorous note explaining why she can't accept a dog, describing how her peacocks behave, sit on tractors, and scream at night.
counterfactuals.output:
# On the Impossibility of Accepting Your Very Kind Offer of a Dog

Dear Neighbor,

I must begin by thanking you for thinking of me when your Labrador produced her regrettable surplus of puppies. I am touched. I am also, I regret to inform you, overruled—by the peacocks.

You see, I did not choose the peacocks. The peacocks chose me, the way a landlord chooses a tenant they intend to torment indefinitely. They arrived three summers ago as "just two, they won't be any trouble," and have since appointed themselves the governing body of this farm. A dog would be a coup, and they do not tolerate coups.

Allow me to describe my colleagues.

They sit on the tractor. Not near the tractor. *On* it. On the seat, on the hood, on the exhaust pipe like tiny feathered dignitaries reviewing a parade that consists entirely of me, walking toward them with a broom, being ignored. When I need to mow, I must first negotiate. Negotiations fail. I mow around a tractor that has become, functionally, a roost.

The male—I call him The Senator—unfurls his tail whenever he wishes to communicate disapproval, which is always. He disapproves of the mail carrier, of my laundry, of clouds. He has strong opinions about clouds.

And then there is the screaming.

I want to be clear that "screaming" is not my dramatization. It is the technical, ornithological, entirely accurate word. At three in the morning, my peacocks produce a sound like a woman being startled by her own ghost. They do this for reasons known only to God, and God, I suspect, has stopped answering. A dog would bark at this. The peacocks would scream at the barking. The dog would howl at the screaming. I would then join in, and the neighbors would finally have grounds to have me committed, which honestly some nights sounds like a spa.

So you understand my position. This household has reached a delicate equilibrium of chaos, and one Labrador—however soft-eared and hopeful—would tip it into open warfare.

Please give the puppy to someone whose tractor is still their own.

With great affection and mild feathers in my coffee,

Your Neighbor
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a quirky personal letter in mid-20th-century Southern style about raising peafowl, why dogs don't fit, and an invitation to come see a peacock before its tail gets ratty.
counterfactuals.output:
Dear Cousin Eugenia,

Well, you have gone and asked me the one question I am never too weary to answer, and that is: how do I get along raising peafowl? The short answer is that I don't get along with them at all. I keep them the way some folks keep a difficult old aunt in the back bedroom — not because it makes a lick of sense, but because the place would go flat and gray without the fuss.

I have got up to eleven of them now, counting the two peahens who sit on their eggs with the sour patience of Baptist deacons and the cock who struts about my yard as though he personally hung the moon and is disappointed in how it turned out. He screams in the night like a woman being murdered slow, and the whole county has learned to sleep through it, which I count as a Christian accomplishment on their part.

You asked why I don't just keep a dog like a normal person, and I will tell you plainly. A dog wants to love you. A dog looks up at you with those wet, forgiving eyes and asks nothing but that you exist, and I find that a terrible burden. A peacock asks for nothing and forgives less. He will not fetch, he will not sit, he will not come when called, and he holds a grudge against my mailman that has lasted the better part of three years. When I walk out to feed him, he does not thank me. He merely turns his back, lifts that great fan of blue and green and gold, and gives me the privilege of admiring his hind parts, which he plainly considers the finest sight I am ever likely to see. And do you know, he may be right.

A dog will greet any fool at the gate. My peacock has taste. He despises the Fuller Brush man, tolerates the preacher, and has decided that Mrs. Hollis from the Missionary Society is a personal enemy, which shows more discernment than I gave him credit for. You cannot buy that kind of company. You can only feed it and stand out of the way.

Now here is the meat of my letter. His tail is at its full glory just now, and glory in a peacock is a passing thing. Come high summer he will molt, and those hundred eyes will drop off one by one until he looks like a dinner fowl that got caught out in a rainstorm, all shabby and ashamed and screaming twice as loud about it. So you must come and see him while he is worth the gasoline.

Come on a Sunday. I will make the ham and you may bring nothing but your admiration, of which he requires a great deal. Do not bring the children if they are inclined to chase, and do not, on your soul, bring a dog.

Your affectionate and slightly deafened cousin,

Miss Louella

P.S. — If you hear tell in town that I have lost my senses keeping such useless creatures, you may confirm it. But mind you add that I have never once been bored.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
